title: Who Deserves the Credit?
paragraphs: The popular version of the penicillin story is tidy: a careless holiday, a stray mould, and a sudden flash of insight that saved millions. The historical record is messier. Alexander Fleming did observe in nineteen twenty eight that a mould contaminating one of his staphylococcus cultures had killed the surrounding bacteria, but his laboratory notebooks are sketchy, and his later accounts of the event contradict one another. Such inconsistencies do not cancel the discovery, but they warn against treating any single version as final.

More importantly, Fleming did not immediately grasp what he had found. He published in nineteen twenty nine, yet for roughly a decade he treated the substance as a possible topical antiseptic rather than an injectable treatment, and it proved difficult to produce in quantity. The decisive work was done at Oxford, where Howard Florey and Ernst Chain assembled a team that learned to purify the drug and showed that it could cure bacterial infections. The gap between a laboratory curiosity and a reliable medicine was therefore wide, and crossing it took years of collective effort.

The Nobel committee recognised this division of labour in nineteen forty five, awarding the prize jointly to all three men. Even so, the award left out Norman Heatley, whose extraction methods made large scale production practical, and Oxford did not award him an honorary doctorate until nineteen ninety. Credit, the episode reminds us, is rarely distributed as evenly as the work deserves. Remembering the whole team gives a more accurate picture than remembering a single hero.
